items.title: Bill Crow interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995
items.q: I fell in love with James Thurber and E.B. White and Alexander Wolcott... that was my beginning of my appreciation of really good writing.

ctx.x: We are filming today for the Hamilton College Jazz Archive and it’s our great pleasure to have with us Bill Crow, who has multiple careers in music, as a bass player and a writer and working with the musicians, which is kind of first for us to be talking in that area, so it will be interesting to hear about how that work is going. Welcome, and I’d love to talk about some of your writing. First of all, can I guess that you were a player before you were a writer?

Yeah, well, I’ve always been interested in writing. I was a big reader when I was a kid, I learned to read before I started grade school. My mother had a little primer and she taught me at home. She also taught me to sing and I guess I inherited my musical ears from her. She was a musician. But I can remember standing by her ironing board singing songs with her before I could see up over the ironing board, so I know I was pretty young. And she tells me that when I still used to take naps in the afternoon in my…

things saw me as a prized student. So they fed me stuff. I think it was a sixth grade teacher that gave me copies of the New Yorker, which I’d never seen before. And I fell in love with James Thurber and E.B. White and Alexander Wolcott, and became quite a sophisticate for the small town that we were in. Some of the terms I didn’t understand at all, I had to go find out what they were talking about, but that was my beginning of my appreciation of really good writing. And I think E.B. White became my hero because…
